finalText:
**Merge** combines two branches by creating a commit that says "these two lines of work came together here." It keeps both branches visible in your history — you can see when they split and when they joined. It's safe because it doesn't rewrite what's already done.

**Rebase** takes your commits and replays them on top of another branch, like you wrote them there all along. It rewrites history to look like a straight line instead of branches. Cleaner to read, but if other people have your commits, you can break their work.

Reach for **merge** when: you're joining long-lived branches (main ← feature), other people are using your commits, or the merge itself is a meaningful event worth recording. Most team repos do this.

Reach for **rebase** when: you're syncing your local branch with main before pushing, you want to clean up a feature branch's history before the merge, or you're the only one using these commits. It's also safe on branches nobody else has pulled.

The middle ground a lot of teams use: rebase locally to stay synced and keep your branch tidy, then merge to main with a merge commit. That way your history on main reads clearly, but your local work wasn't messy.
